opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the clearest way to describe the limitation is with an analogy we use a lot: current large language models are a bit like a patient with anterograde amnesia. They have a large store of knowledge from pre-training, which is a kind of long-term memory frozen in the past. They also have their immediate context window, which works like short-term memory. But there's almost nothing in between. Once something falls out of the context window, it's gone. The model can't consolidate new experience into lasting knowledge the way we do.

So after deployment, these models are essentially static. You can give them information in context and they'll use it impressively through in-context learning, but that learning is temporary. It doesn't change the underlying parameters, and it doesn't build up over time. The two main ways we update them, retraining or fine-tuning, are expensive, happen offline, and often cause catastrophic forgetting.

The second limitation is more conceptual. We've treated architecture and optimization as two separate things: you design a network, then you train it with an optimizer. Most progress has come from stacking more layers and scaling up. But depth in that sense doesn't necessarily give you more expressive learning ability. It doesn't let the model learn at different levels of abstraction or on different timescales.

Nested Learning came from asking what happens if we stop drawing that line. If you look closely, an optimizer like momentum is itself a small associative memory that compresses gradients. Attention is a memory that maps keys to values. Even the feed-forward layers can be viewed as memory modules that are just updated very slowly. So you can see a model as a system of nested optimization problems, each with its own context flow and its own update frequency.

The brain does something similar. It has oscillations at different frequencies, and memory consolidation happens across multiple timescales, some fast and online, some slower, for example during sleep. Today's LLMs have basically two frequencies: "updated every token" and "never updated after training." Our view is that the missing piece is a continuum of memory between those extremes. That's what we think could get us toward models that genuinely keep learning, rather than just performing in-context tricks on top of a frozen core.

r001.rationale: It says retraining and fine-tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting, presenting that as a problem with updating models to incorporate new experience.

r002.rationale: It describes pre-training knowledge as frozen in the past, but does not link a knowledge cutoff or newer knowledge to the need to update parameters.

r003.rationale: It calls retraining and fine-tuning expensive, but does not identify repeatedly updating all model parameters as the obstacle.

r004.rationale: It says context learning is temporary and does not change parameters, and that new experience needs to be consolidated into lasting knowledge.

r005.rationale: It explicitly says information is gone once it falls out of the context window, which it characterizes as short-term memory.

r006.rationale: It mentions learning at different levels of abstraction, but does not characterize abstraction learning as compressing data into explanatory patterns.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the biggest limitation of current LLMs is that they're frozen after training. We spend an enormous amount of compute to pretrain a model, and then at deployment it essentially stops learning. Whatever it knows is baked into the weights at a single snapshot in time, and the only mechanism it has to use new information is the context window. That's fundamentally different from how humans or even simple animals work. We keep learning continuously, we consolidate experiences into long-term memory, and we don't lose everything we knew before.

So you have this gap. On one side there's in-context learning, which is fast and flexible but ephemeral, and it's bounded by whatever you can fit into the context. On the other side there's pretraining or fine-tuning, which actually changes the parameters, but it's slow, expensive, and suffers from catastrophic forgetting. Everything in between is basically missing. There's no principled way for a model to take something it saw an hour ago and integrate it into its parameters at an intermediate timescale.

The second thing I'd point to is architectural. When you look at a Transformer, people describe it as a single model with a single optimizer sitting outside of it. But if you look more carefully, that distinction is somewhat artificial. Attention is itself doing a kind of learning at inference time, associating keys and values. The optimizer, with momentum and so on, is itself a kind of memory of past gradients. Once you see that, a lot of the components we treat as separate, the architecture and the training algorithm, start to look like the same thing: nested systems that compress information from a stream of data, each at its own frequency of update.

And I think the reason we've hit a plateau in some respects is that we've been treating depth as stacking layers, all updated at the same rate, with one global objective. There's no notion of different levels of the system learning at different timescales, which is exactly what the brain seems to do with things like fast synaptic changes and slow consolidation. So Nested Learning started from asking: what if we take that multi-level, multi-timescale view seriously, and design models where learning is built into the architecture rather than something that only happens offline? That reframing gives you a way to think about continual learning, long-term memory, and even what the optimizer should be, all in one unified picture.

r001.rationale: It says parameter-changing pretraining or fine-tuning suffers from catastrophic forgetting, making it harder to incorporate new information while retaining prior knowledge.

r002.rationale: It describes models as frozen after training and contrasts context use with parameter updates, but does not connect knowledge cutoffs to updating parameters with newer knowledge.

r003.rationale: It calls pretraining and fine-tuning slow and expensive, but does not identify repeatedly updating all parameters of a large model as the obstacle.

r004.rationale: It says there is no principled way to integrate something seen an hour ago into the model’s parameters, directly identifying the need to move knowledge beyond context.

r005.rationale: It says in-context learning is bounded by what fits in the context window, limiting knowledge kept in token space.

r006.rationale: It describes nested systems as compressing information, but does not characterize learning abstractions as compression into underlying explanatory patterns.

astra-6.text:
I think the central limitation is the separation between training and deployment. During training, a model changes its parameters and learns from data. But once we deploy it, those parameters are typically fixed. It can adapt through the context we give it, but that adaptation doesn’t automatically become a lasting change in the model. Having a long context window and continually learning are different capabilities.

That creates a dilemma. We want models to learn from new experiences, but updating their parameters can interfere with what they already know. So the question is not simply, “How do we keep training?” It’s, “How do we incorporate new information while preserving useful knowledge, and how do we decide what should persist?”

The perspective behind Nested Learning is to think about learning at multiple timescales. Some information should change our behavior immediately and then disappear. Other information should accumulate slowly and become more stable. Instead of treating a model as one system with a single learning process, we can think about interacting learning processes, each with its own way of updating and retaining information.

From that perspective, the limitation isn’t necessarily the next-token prediction objective itself. It’s also how we organize memory and adaptation around that objective. We want systems that can keep learning from experience, rather than relying primarily on a fixed set of parameters plus a temporary context.

r001.rationale: It says parameter updates made to learn from new experiences can interfere with what the model already knows, identifying that interference as an obstacle.

r002.rationale: It does not mention knowledge cutoffs or the need to update parameters to incorporate newer knowledge.

r003.rationale: It does not identify the cost of repeatedly updating all parameters of a large model.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes temporary context from lasting parameter changes, but does not clearly argue that knowledge must be transferred from context into parameters.

r005.rationale: It contrasts long context with continual learning but does not identify finite context length as a limitation.

r006.rationale: It does not characterize abstraction learning as compressing data into underlying explanatory patterns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main limitation is that we’ve separated learning and inference too sharply. During training, a model updates its parameters and accumulates knowledge. But when we deploy it, those parameters are usually frozen. The model can adapt through its context, but that adaptation is temporary and constrained by what fits in the context window. It doesn’t necessarily become a lasting part of the model.

So you have this very powerful system that can learn from a huge training corpus, but doesn’t have an equally effective mechanism for continually learning from its own stream of experience. If you try to solve that simply by continuing to train it, you run into issues like catastrophic forgetting: learning something new can interfere with what it already knows.

The motivation for Nested Learning is to look at these as connected problems. We can think of a model as a collection of learning processes operating at different timescales. Some components adapt very quickly to the immediate input; others update more slowly and preserve more persistent knowledge. From that perspective, architecture and optimization aren’t completely separate things. Both determine how information gets stored, updated, and retrieved.

The question becomes: how do we build a system that can absorb new information, retain what matters, and keep learning without having to start over? That’s the direction we’re trying to explore.

r001.rationale: It says that continuing to train can cause catastrophic forgetting, where new learning interferes with what the model already knows.

r002.rationale: It does not mention knowledge cutoffs or connect newer knowledge to updating model parameters.

r003.rationale: It does not identify the cost of repeatedly updating all parameters as an obstacle.

r004.rationale: It describes context-based adaptation as temporary and asks how to retain new information, but does not clearly argue that knowledge must be transferred from context into model parameters.

r005.rationale: It says context-based adaptation is constrained by what fits in the context window, limiting how much information can be retained there.

r006.rationale: It discusses learning at different timescales, but does not characterize abstraction learning as compressing data into explanatory patterns.
